title: Would Jesus Oppose the Resurrection Gospel? Kingdom, Mercy, and the Authority of Easter
heading: The teacher as a critic of his own reception
text: What if Jesus encountered the religion that developed around him and objected to what it had made most important? The question is sharper than asking whether a miracle occurred. Imagine a historical Jesus reading Luke's account of his disappearance at Emmaus and his subsequent meal of fish before frightened disciples. Suppose, for the sake of the thought experiment, that he regarded those scenes as untrue. Why might he consider them harmful as teaching, rather than merely inaccurate as biography? Could they redirect people away from the life he wanted them to lead? This is the central question raised by Micah Blumberg's November 2026 materials. It asks about a possible conflict between fidelity to Jesus and fidelity to later claims about Jesus. The hypothesis deserves development on its own terms. Merely saying that resurrection belongs to Christian orthodoxy does not answer whether the historical teacher would have endorsed every subsequent expression of that orthodoxy. The strongest form of the objection has three parts: 1. A community might make assent to a miraculous event the decisive test of faith while treating mercy, reconciliation, and care for the poor as secondary. 2. It might elevate the messenger into an object of allegiance in ways that protect its authorities from the messenger's own criticism of power. 3. It might turn forgiveness into a transaction requiring an innocent death, obscuring the generosity expressed in Jesus's teaching about repentance and restored relationships. Each possibility concerns what a doctrine does in a community. The objection remains intelligible whether a resurrection account is interpreted literally, symbolically, or through some combination of the two. A true claim can be used to avoid an obligation. An imaginative story can also intensify that obligation. The ethical question cannot be answered by the historical question alone. There is an important limit already present in Micah's inquiry. He explicitly objects to treating an individual resurrection as necessarily contradicting or replacing a collective resurrection: “I don't think this one is a clear contradiction or a clear replacement.” That qualification improves the argument. The chapter therefore does not claim that Jesus must have rejected resurrection because one person was said to rise before others. Its central concern is a possible change in priorities, authority, and the meaning of forgiveness. This is a reconstructed objection, not a recovered speech by Jesus. The Gospel traditions used to reconstruct his priorities were themselves transmitted by communities that believed in his resurrection. We cannot simply label the passages we admire historical and the passages we dislike later invention. But those traditions preserve enough internal tension to make the question worth asking.

title: Would Jesus Oppose the Resurrection Gospel? Kingdom, Mercy, and the Authority of Easter
heading: What “resurrection gospel” means here
text: Several different teachings are often gathered under this phrase: - God raised and vindicated Jesus after his execution. - The same Jesus entered an imperishable embodied existence. - Jesus returned to ordinary biological life, like a resuscitated patient. - Jesus's death and resurrection make salvation possible. - Acceptance of a particular explanation of these events determines who belongs, while conduct matters less. These claims do not entail one another. Rejecting mere resuscitation does not reject every account of bodily resurrection. Rejecting a punitive theory of atonement does not require rejecting Easter. Affirming resurrection does not logically make ethics dispensable. Paul already distinguishes resurrection from a return to ordinary mortality. In Romans 6, the risen Christ no longer dies; that claim becomes the basis for a changed life among believers. The passage combines an event, an enduring transformation, and a present ethical demand. Romans 6:1–14 The thought experiment is consequently strongest when its target is specified: Would Jesus oppose a form of resurrection-centered Christianity that made claims about his supernatural status a substitute for the kingdom-shaped life he taught? A more ambitious question, whether he would reject every resurrection proclamation about himself, requires further evidence that we do not possess.

title: Would Jesus Oppose the Resurrection Gospel? Kingdom, Mercy, and the Authority of Easter
heading: The earliest evidence does not settle Jesus's approval
text: The companion chapter on early resurrection accounts examines the chronology and textual history in detail. Two distinctions matter here. First, the surviving evidence for resurrection belief is earlier than the narrative Gospels. First Corinthians is usually placed in the 50s CE. Mark is commonly dated around 70, and Luke often around 80–90, although dates remain debated. These are dates of surviving compositions, not dates on which every tradition they contain originated. The claim that all the relevant witnesses first appeared at least sixty years after Jesus therefore overstates the gap. USCCB introductions to 1 Corinthians, Mark, and Luke In 1 Corinthians 15:3–11, Paul presents death, burial, resurrection, and appearances as received tradition. He connects the proclamation with Cephas, the Twelve, James, and other apostles, as well as himself. His own letter to the Galatians also describes meeting Cephas and James. These are early textual claims about the movement's beliefs and relationships. They do not independently verify a miracle, establish every detail of the appearance list, or give us Jesus's assessment of the proclamation. 1 Corinthians 15:3–11; Galatians 1:18–20 Second, the secondary ending of Mark is a real textual-critical finding with a limited consequence. Mark 16:9–20 supplies appearances absent from the surviving account ending at 16:8. Yet Mark 16:1–8 already presents an empty tomb, an announcement that Jesus has been raised, and a promise of a Galilean encounter. Removing the longer ending does not remove resurrection from Mark. Whether the abrupt ending at 16:8 was intentional or an earlier continuation was lost is a separate question. Mark 16 and its textual notes The more defensible critical argument is therefore not that resurrection was wholly absent until late scribes invented it. It is that an early conviction could acquire new narrative forms, bodily specifications, and institutional uses. Being early does not prove being authorized by Jesus. Equally, being later does not prove being unfaithful to him. Those judgments require comparison of content and purpose.

title: Would Jesus Oppose the Resurrection Gospel? Kingdom, Mercy, and the Authority of Easter
heading: Signs: when evidence becomes a substitute for response
text: The strongest objection The sign-refusal traditions give the thought experiment an identifiable textual starting point. In Mark 8:11–13, opponents request a heavenly sign as a test, and Jesus refuses. In Luke 16:19–31, the rich man's neglect of Lazarus is followed by a warning that even someone returning from the dead would not persuade people who refuse to hear Moses and the prophets. Mark 8:11–13; Luke 16:19–31 Read together, these passages support a serious criticism of religious spectatorship. A person can demand extraordinary evidence while failing to respond to an ordinary, visible human need. The poor man was already at the rich man's gate. The failure was not a shortage of spectacular information. Applied to Easter, the objection becomes: why should accepting an account of a vanished body or a meal of fish excuse indifference to the person outside the door? If resurrection preaching becomes a way of ranking people by assent while tolerating cruelty, it can frustrate the moral response that the sign-refusal tradition demands. This version is stronger than saying Jesus opposed all observable miracles. It identifies a misuse of evidence: making the extraordinary a reason to postpone what is already required. The counterevidence within the same traditions Mark places the refusal of a demanded sign in a narrative full of healings and feedings. More pointedly, Mark 2:1–12 presents a healing as evidence of the Son of Man's authority to forgive. A universal rule that Jesus never used miraculous acts to establish authority cannot be extracted from these texts without setting aside substantial counterevidence. Mark 2:1–12 Matthew also gives the sign of Jonah an explicit relation to the Son of Man's time in the earth. Luke's version emphasizes Jonah's role and the Ninevites' repentance rather than supplying Matthew's three-day comparison. The differing versions allow historical questions about development. They also show that the surviving sign tradition cannot simply be quoted as an uncontested ban on resurrection as a sign. Matthew 12:38–42; Luke 11:29–32 Luke 24 is not a public performance offered on demand to hostile spectators. It concerns followers struggling with recognition, fear, and disbelief. At Emmaus, scripture and shared bread precede recognition. The chapter's commission concerns repentance and forgiveness, not instructions to reproduce a bodily experiment. John likewise ends the Thomas episode by blessing people who believe without seeing. Luke 24:13–49; John 20:24–29 These differences do not require a reader to accept the scenes as historical. They change the interpretation being criticized. Luke can be read as connecting recognition to renewed witness and action. The contradiction emerges most clearly when later readers isolate the physical demonstration from that purpose and make it the whole message.

title: Would Jesus Oppose the Resurrection Gospel? Kingdom, Mercy, and the Authority of Easter
heading: The kingdom and the messenger
text: Could worship conceal disobedience? The ethical challenge has unusually strong support in sayings addressed to Jesus's own followers. Luke 6:46 questions calling Jesus Lord while refusing to do what he says. Matthew 7:21–23 rejects verbal allegiance and even claims of prophecy and mighty works when accompanied by wrongdoing. These texts do not merely criticize outsiders who fail to believe. They criticize religious insiders whose declarations exceed their conduct. Luke 6:46–49; Matthew 7:21–23 The rich man's encounter in Mark makes the issue concrete. Jesus directs him toward commandments, release of wealth to the poor, and following. The man's attachment to possessions is the obstacle. Luke's blessings and woes, together with the command to love enemies, similarly locate the kingdom within changed relationships rather than a merely private religious opinion. Mark 10:17–31; Luke 6:20–36 Matthew 25:31–46 joins judgment to feeding, welcoming, clothing, and visiting. Scholars and churches differ about the precise identity of the “least” in this passage, including whether the primary reference is to vulnerable disciples. Even with that question left open, the scene does not depict correct supernatural description as sufficient. Response to vulnerable persons matters. Matthew 25:31–46 and notes The reconstructed criticism is therefore credible: honoring a teacher's name while neutralizing the teacher's demands can become a form of betrayal. A community might defend the reality of Jesus's body while neglecting the bodies of hungry people. Its confidence about Easter would not answer the accusation. The kingdom cannot be reduced to modern humanitarianism The historical reconstruction also needs restraint. The kingdom traditions concern God's action, judgment, and a transformed order, alongside ethical conduct. A first-century Jewish apocalyptic prophet need not resemble a modern secular moral philosopher. Mark 12 portrays Jesus defending resurrection against its opponents, not merely using afterlife language as a metaphor for kindness. Mark 12:18–27 Nor does Mark 10:18, where Jesus directs attention to God's goodness, by itself settle every question about Jesus's self-understanding. In the same conversation he calls the man to follow him. The argument that Jesus's message was God-directed is much stronger than the claim that he assigned himself no distinctive authority. Both aspects of the text must be considered. Mark 10:17–22 Paul and Luke supply their own answer Paul does not abandon God's kingdom in 1 Corinthians 15. Christ's resurrection initiates a sequence culminating in the defeat of hostile powers and death, the handing over of the kingdom to God, and the Son's own subjection to God. That is a substantial transformation of messianic expectation, but its stated goal is larger than admiration for an isolated miracle-worker. 1 Corinthians 15:20–28 Luke's second volume makes a similarly important connection. Acts 4:32–35 places testimony to the resurrection beside shared possessions and distribution according to need. Whatever the historical accuracy of this idealized portrait, the author's literary intention is incompatible with saying that concern for material need has simply vanished. Dale Martin's account of Luke likewise identifies reversal of earthly status and concern for the lowly as major organizing themes. Acts 4:32–35; Martin, Yale lecture on Luke The conflict is consequently not an exhaustive opposition between Jesus's ethics and everyone else's belief. A resurrection believer can answer that God vindicates the very life and mission the critic wants to recover. The critic must then ask whether this connection actually governs teaching and practice. The believer must answer with more than a declaration that it ought to.

title: Would Jesus Oppose the Resurrection Gospel? Kingdom, Mercy, and the Authority of Easter
heading: Mercy, sacrifice, and what forgiveness requires
text: The alternative already present in Jesus traditions The Lord's Prayer links a request for divine forgiveness with forgiveness of others. The returning son in Luke 15 is received through the father's compassion, without a narrative requirement that someone first endure punishment in his place. The calf killed for the celebration is a feast, not a stated expiatory price paid to secure the father's welcome. Matthew's appeal to Hosea places mercy at the center of Jesus's fellowship with sinners. Luke 11:2–4; Luke 15:11–32; Matthew 9:9–13 These traditions support a theological question: if forgiveness is already enacted through compassion, repentance, and reconciliation, why should Jesus's execution become a necessary payment before God is able or willing to forgive? An interpretation that makes mercy dependent on satisfying a demand for suffering may appear to reverse the movement of these stories. Adriana Destro and Mauro Pesce offer a scholarly formulation relevant to this concern. They interpret the forgiveness teaching in Matthew 6:12 as a relationship among God, the person forgiven, and the person that individual must forgive, with social consequences involving reconciliation and debt. Crucially, they do not infer that Jesus rejected all Temple sacrificial ritual. Their argument distinguishes access to forgiveness from a universal abolition of sacrifice. Destro and Pesce, “Between family and temple: Jesus and sacrifices” That distinction preserves the strongest objection without manufacturing a simple contrast between a merciful Jesus and an inherently merciless Judaism. Hosea's criticism is itself Jewish scripture. Mark's scribe can say that love of God and neighbor exceeds burnt offerings, and Jesus approves his understanding. Matthew also depicts Jesus telling a worshiper to reconcile and then return to the altar with the gift. Prioritizing mercy does not automatically eliminate the altar. Mark 12:28–34; Matthew 5:23–24 Paula Fredriksen's critique of modern reconstructions is pertinent here: ritual impurity, moral wrongdoing, and exclusion from divine mercy are not interchangeable categories. Her argument challenges portrayals that make Jesus's Jewish setting into a uniformly oppressive system so that his compassion can appear unprecedented. This does not eliminate conflict over Temple authority. It requires the nature of the conflict to be demonstrated. Fredriksen, “Did Jesus Oppose the Purity Laws?” What the sacrificial critique must still explain The opposite simplification would be to treat every connection between suffering and communal restoration as foreign to Jewish thought. In 2 Maccabees 7:37–38, a martyr offers his life in faithfulness to ancestral law and asks that the brothers' suffering bring an end to divine wrath against their people. This is not a Christian doctrine of the cross, but it is counterevidence to the assertion that interpreting a righteous death as beneficial for others was inconceivable within Judaism. 2 Maccabees 7:37–38 The Gospel tradition itself contains the ransom saying in Mark 10:45 and covenantal blood language in Mark 14:24. Paul preserves a meal tradition involving body and covenantal blood in 1 Corinthians 11:23–26. Their relationship to Jesus's historical self-understanding remains a question for source criticism. They cannot be dismissed merely because a reconstructed Jesus has already been defined as incapable of saying anything like them. Mark 10:35–45; Mark 14:22–25; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26 Even within Torah, a universal equation between forgiveness and a new act of bloodshed is too blunt: Leviticus permits a poor person's flour offering in a specified sin-offering provision. That does not abolish the sacrificial system. It shows why a claim about what God invariably requires cannot be assumed from a slogan about blood. Leviticus 5:11; Leviticus 5:12–13 Most importantly, resurrection and penal substitution are different claims. One concerns God's action toward the dead Jesus. The other explains salvation through punishment borne on others' behalf. An account of resurrection as vindication, liberation, or victory over death need not make God a creditor whose willingness to forgive depends on violence. The proposed objection should therefore name its target: a theology that makes violence the precondition of mercy, or that uses Jesus's suffering to excuse fresh suffering. It should not imply that rejecting this theology automatically refutes every Christian interpretation of the cross or resurrection.

title: Would Jesus Oppose the Resurrection Gospel? Kingdom, Mercy, and the Authority of Easter
heading: Paul's spiritual body and Luke's flesh and bones
text: The difference in emphasis is real. Paul develops resurrection through contrasts between perishability and imperishability, weakness and power, earthly and heavenly existence. Luke gives a narrative in which Jesus is recognizable, tangible, and able to eat. The critical question is whether the latter elaborates the former, materially revises it, or represents another strand of early belief. We should not decide that question by translating “spiritual” into the modern word “imaginary.” 1 Corinthians 15:35–54; Luke 24:36–43 There is a real scholarly disagreement Dale Martin interprets Paul's pneumatic body through ancient understandings of spirit as a kind of substance. On this reading, the risen body differs profoundly from ordinary fleshly embodiment without being equivalent to an immaterial idea or a surviving reputation. Martin, Yale lecture on Paul Peter Lampe emphasizes whole-person transformation, but his account differs from Martin's compositional reading of spirit. For Lampe, “spiritual” identifies God's creative agency, not the new body's material constitution. Resurrection is not a return to ordinary mortal embodiment. Yet he leaves unresolved whether it reuses transformed matter from the old body, considering arguments for continuity as well as discontinuity. His ethical reading also ties salvation to embodied conduct. Lampe, “Paul's Concept of a Spiritual Body,” especially pp. 108–114 James P. Ware argues for a stronger continuity: the once-mortal body is raised and transformed, with the repeated subject of Paul's sowing-and-raising contrasts carrying argumentative weight. His account interprets the adjectives in terms of the body's animating life rather than treating spirit as the replacement for the earthly body. This is a substantive exegetical alternative, not a point that can be settled by one English phrase. Ware, “Jesus's Resurrection according to Paul the Apostle” The chapter therefore preserves the question about development instead of harmonizing Paul and Luke in advance. It also declines to state that scholars have proved Paul meant a nonbodily vision while Luke invented embodiment. The disagreement includes what “body” and “spirit” meant in ancient discourse, the kind of continuity Paul intended, and how later narratives relate to it. What the narratives actually claim Luke's Emmaus episode combines recognition with disappearance. John combines locked doors with recognition through wounds. Neither scene depicts an uncomplicated return to the same limitations as ordinary mortal life. John says that Jesus appears when the doors are locked; it does not narrate him physically passing through wood. John offers Thomas the opportunity to touch, but does not say that Thomas actually does so. Such details matter when the argument concerns what an author has added. Luke 24:30–43; John 20:19–29 Nor can the historical cause of the bodily emphasis simply be announced as fear of Gnostics. An anti-docetic interpretation, meaning an answer to claims that Jesus only seemed human, has been influential. J. D. Atkins's study of early reception challenges its automatic application to Luke and John and emphasizes prophetic fulfillment. His argument is evidence of a live interpretive dispute, not a new consensus that settles the question in the other direction. Atkins, The Doubt of the Apostles and the Resurrection Faith of the Early Church, abstract Deborah Thompson Prince supplies a further literary comparison. Ancient apparition stories did not all obey a single rule that ghosts could never eat or be touched. She argues that Luke draws on several kinds of postmortem appearance while exceeding the expectations attached to any one of them. This supports examining the scenes as purposeful ancient storytelling rather than reading them as straightforward modern tests of biology. It does not, by itself, prove that Luke copied a particular story or that Jesus would have rejected his portrayal. Prince, “The ‘Ghost’ of Jesus,” especially pp. 296–298 Paul's placement of his own appearance alongside earlier appearances is also significant without being conclusive about their sensory character. It gives them a common place in his argument for apostolic witness. It does not describe each experience closely enough to establish that every witness saw, heard, or touched the same things in the same way. The detailed Damascus-road accounts are in Acts, not in Paul's own version of the list. 1 Corinthians 15:3–11; Galatians 1:15–17 The ethical question survives all three major possibilities. If Luke expanded an earlier spiritual conception, we can ask what the expansion teaches. If Luke intended transformed embodiment continuous with Paul's proclamation, we can ask how bodily vindication serves the kingdom. If both preserve different interpretations, we can ask which conception best sustains the obligations they claim to authorize.

title: Would Jesus Oppose the Resurrection Gospel? Kingdom, Mercy, and the Authority of Easter
heading: Why an individual resurrection is not the decisive contradiction
text: Jewish resurrection hopes were varied. Daniel 12 connects awakening from the dust with judgment and shining like the heavens. Second Maccabees 7 includes the hope of receiving mutilated bodily members again. These are not identical descriptions, and neither licenses a claim that all Jews possessed one detailed account of resurrection mechanics. Daniel 12:1–3; 2 Maccabees 7:9–14 In Mark 12:25, being like angels directly answers a question about marriage after resurrection. It does not explicitly settle whether resurrected persons could eat, bear recognizable features, or appear to the living. Reading a complete physiology into that comparison goes beyond the statement. Nor does agreement with a Pharisaic position on resurrection establish that Jesus formally belonged to the Pharisees. Mark 12:18–27 Paul's firstfruits image supplies the clearest reason to preserve Micah's qualification. Jesus's rising is presented as the beginning of the expected harvest, followed by others, rather than a private exception that cancels their future. It is a reinterpretation of timing and messianic significance. Calling it logically impossible within every Jewish framework would make that judgment before examining the interpretation itself. 1 Corinthians 15:20–28 There may still be a historically important innovation here. Innovation and contradiction are different propositions. Neither, by itself, establishes Jesus's approval or opposition.

title: Would Jesus Oppose the Resurrection Gospel? Kingdom, Mercy, and the Authority of Easter
heading: Did Jesus predict the story later told about him?
text: The traditional reply is straightforward: the Gospels depict Jesus predicting his suffering and resurrection, so the Easter proclamation completes his intention. This is a coherent reading of the narratives. It is not yet an independent historical demonstration that the narrated predictions reproduce his words. Mark 10:32–34 anticipates details of the later passion sequence. Such close correspondence invites the possibility of retrospective shaping, or vaticinium ex eventu, prophecy after the event. Bart Ehrman argues that these predictions are best understood as later portrayals of a Jesus who knew what would happen, rather than secure reports of his own expectations. That is a specific critical judgment, not a unanimous verdict. The disciples' fear and failure to understand also raise a question about whether a precise timetable had actually been communicated. Mark 10:32–34; Ehrman, public response on the passion predictions But the argument from confusion is not decisive. The same author can use predictions and incomprehension together to dramatize the disciples' failure. A narrative's portrayal of frightened followers is not an independent psychological record with which to prove that another part of the narrative never happened. Nor does questioning detailed predictions prove that Jesus could not anticipate danger, death, divine vindication, or some combination of them. Craig A. Evans offers a useful counterposition: he acknowledges details that suggest editing after the events, while arguing that other sayings support Jesus's anticipation of suffering and death. Retrospective elaboration and an earlier expectation of danger are not mutually exclusive. Evans, “Prophet, Sage, Healer, Messiah, and Martyr,” pp. 1239–1242 Three questions should remain distinct: whether Jesus expected a violent death; whether he interpreted that death as part of his mission; and whether he supplied the detailed resurrection predictions now present in the Gospels. An answer to one does not automatically answer the others. The strongest reply to an overly confident conservative argument is consequently methodological: citing the prediction proves that an evangelist attributed foresight to Jesus, while its historical origin still needs investigation. The strongest reply to an overly confident skeptical argument is symmetrical: identifying retrospective theology does not prove that no earlier expectation contributed to it. This leaves the central question open. Even a Jesus who expected vindication might oppose uses of his story that displaced mercy. Even a Jesus who did not expect personal resurrection might have been remembered by followers who believed they had encountered him and understood those experiences through Jewish scripture. Neither possibility can be settled simply by declaring the other psychologically impossible.

title: Would Jesus Oppose the Resurrection Gospel? Kingdom, Mercy, and the Authority of Easter
heading: John, Qumran, and the wider archive
text: Micah's inquiry also asks whether the canonical portrait should be tested against traditions outside the later New Testament collection. That move is valuable when it expands the comparison rather than assigning authenticity according to whether a text was excluded. The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve a varied Jewish archive, including manuscripts that predate the usual first-century setting of Jesus. The Israel Antiquities Authority dates the Qumran manuscripts broadly from the third century BCE to the first century CE. Those dates belong to particular manuscripts and collections, not automatically to every idea in every later work with similar language. IAA, introduction to the Scrolls There are substantial comparisons with Johannine language. Marie-Émile Boismard identifies affinities between the Community Rule's language of light, darkness, truth, and opposing spirits and the First Epistle of John. His argument concerns particular texts and patterns, with ethical conduct central to the comparison. It should not be silently converted into proof that the author or community of the Gospel of John had existed for two or three centuries before Jesus. The Gospel and First Epistle are related literary objects, not interchangeable evidence. Boismard, “The First Epistle of John and the Writings of Qumran” Jörg Frey's methodological treatment emphasizes how the Scrolls reveal the variety of Jewish traditions from which New Testament language becomes intelligible, while warning against treating Qumran as simply the early Christian community under another name. This permits several hypotheses: shared scriptural inheritance, wider Jewish vocabulary, specific literary influence, or contact between groups. Continuous institutional identity is a stronger proposition requiring additional evidence. Frey, “The Relevance of the Dead Sea Scrolls for New Testament Interpretation,” pp. 86–99 The wiki's Jesus–Teacher of Righteousness hypothesis and earlier-teacher and displaced-biography inquiry explore a stronger reconstruction. They remain distinct from this chapter's provisional first-century thought experiment. Evidence for old symbols or textual transmission would not alone establish identity between persons or relocation of a biography. The Nag Hammadi material complicates any binary between canonical miracle religion and noncanonical ethics. The Gospel of Thomas gives interpretive attention to sayings rather than a passion-and-Easter narrative, but its dating and relationship to the canonical Gospels remain debated. A collection's literary focus cannot establish that its author rejected every belief it leaves unnarrated. Christopher W. Skinner, NASSCAL entry on Thomas The Treatise on Resurrection offers a different case: a Christian spiritual interpretation that retains resurrection rather than discarding it. Melissa Harl Sellew's introduction places the work in the late second century and describes an intellectual-spiritual transformation with implications for present life and postmortem existence. It supplies a historical alternative to one understanding of fleshly resurrection, not a direct report of Jesus's own objection to Easter. Sellew, introduction to Treatise on Resurrection Likewise, “the Ethiopian library” needs to become a set of named works, manuscripts, and interpretive traditions before it can support a historical claim. Survival in an Ethiopian collection can be crucial evidence of transmission. It does not automatically establish an earlier composition or a message closer to Jesus. The comparison of the living Jesus in Thomas, John, and the Synoptics and inquiry into truth across canonical and Gnostic Gospels provide places to develop these distinctions.

title: Would Jesus Oppose the Resurrection Gospel? Kingdom, Mercy, and the Authority of Easter
heading: A faith that answers the teacher
text: The hypothesis has now become more precise. We cannot establish that the historical Jesus would have rejected all belief in his resurrection. We can reconstruct a strong objection to versions of that belief that excuse disobedience, monopolize access to God, or treat forgiveness as permission to leave harm unrepaired. That objection need not be directed only against later orthodoxy. A symbolic or Gnostic interpretation could also become an elite claim to special knowledge detached from care. Paul himself opposes a community in which some eat abundantly while others go hungry, and he makes the shared meal's meaning answerable to that failure. His language about Christ's death does not spare believers scrutiny of their treatment of one another. 1 Corinthians 11:17–34 Nor is Paul's faith merely an easy intellectual assent contrasted with Jesus's difficult action. Galatians 5 connects faith with love and presents the Spirit's life through patience, generosity, gentleness, and self-control. Paul also appeals to teachings attributed to the Lord on marriage and the support of messengers. His letters are selective and give little narrative biography, but that is different from proving total indifference to Jesus's teaching. Galatians 5:6, 13–26; 1 Corinthians 7:10–12; 1 Corinthians 9:14 The decisive constructive test is therefore how interpretation directs a life: - Does it make reconciliation, truthfulness, and care more demanding, or provide a way around them? - Does it treat bodily suffering as something to remedy, or as an acceptable price for another person's religious project? - Does it permit claims of authority to be questioned when their consequences contradict the teaching they invoke? - Does it distinguish what a text says, what a historian can infer, what a community hopes, and what a believer chooses to affirm? These questions extend Christic Self-Formation Theory and Scripture, power and the work of repair. They also give the companion inquiry into Christianity after bodily resurrection a stricter criterion. Removing a literal belief does not automatically produce a more faithful or compassionate community. Preserving it does not automatically preserve the teacher's priorities. The most defensible conclusion is conditional but substantial: a resurrection gospel that substitutes allegiance to Jesus for the life Jesus commands can be criticized from within the Jesus traditions themselves. Whether Jesus would reject resurrection proclamation as such remains an unresolved historical counterfactual. Whether Christian communities use it to practice or evade mercy is a question that their conduct can help answer.

title: Would Jesus Oppose the Resurrection Gospel? Kingdom, Mercy, and the Authority of Easter
heading: Provenance and reading boundaries
text: This chapter develops Micah Blumberg's question and two supplied texts of November 5, 2026. The attachments contain an exploratory question, explicit qualifications, and unattributed explanatory passages. Those passages are treated as proposals to examine, not independent scholarly authorities or a definitive statement of his settled beliefs. The chapter preserves his qualification about individual and collective resurrection and does not overwrite earlier inquiries that consider reconciliation between literal belief and inward transformation. The reconstructed objections are newly developed argument, not quotations of the historical Jesus. The chapter's main historical setting is the conventional first-century reconstruction used in the supplied thought experiment. The wiki's earlier-founder hypotheses remain separate investigations. Authorial working edition developed with AI assistance. Original conversation records and this developed argument remain distinct. Biblical citations point to primary texts in English translation, principally the public-domain American Standard Version and the NABRE hosted by the USCCB. They establish what those texts say, not independent verification of the events they report. Modern summaries are distinguished from primary texts. No claim of universal scholarly agreement is made for interpretations represented by individual scholars.

title: Early resurrection accounts and source criticism
heading: The question behind the sequence
text: My starting question is whether the resurrection stories changed as Christianity developed. Paul speaks about a spiritual body. Mark, in its earliest recoverable ending, does not narrate an encounter with the risen Jesus. Matthew, Luke and John tell more extensive appearance stories, including bodily contact and, in Luke, eating. What happened between these accounts? Did later Christians give an increasingly tangible form to an earlier experience of revelation? The original proposal in Paul and the Resurrection was stronger: an early spiritual resurrection was subsequently replaced by a resurrection of the flesh. Biblical Resurrection Interpretations presses the objection that simply calling both accounts “embodied” can hide an important difference. That objection deserves a serious comparison. “Body” is not a sufficient explanation if the texts imagine different kinds of body. The comparison must also allow the evidence to complicate the proposal. A later surviving story does not necessarily describe a later-invented belief. A spiritual body does not necessarily mean an immaterial soul. An account of what Paul believed does not establish what happened to Jesus. These distinctions make it possible to investigate development without assuming either perfect agreement or a predetermined sequence of fabrication. This chapter studies the historical and textual question. Christianity After Bodily Resurrection? considers the separate theological question of what faith and Christian formation might become when people cannot affirm bodily resurrection literally.

title: Early resurrection accounts and source criticism
heading: Begin with documents, not a reconstructed film
text: First Corinthians belongs to the 50s CE. It is earlier than the surviving canonical Gospels and is a letter addressing particular communities and disputes. The USCCB introduction places it around 56 and identifies its Pauline authorship as secure. Its age makes it indispensable, but a letter is not an exhaustive account of everything its author or audience knew. Introduction to 1 Corinthians. A conventional critical chronology places Mark around 70, Matthew and Luke commonly in the 80s or 90s, and John toward the end of the first century. The exact dates, especially the dating of Luke–Acts and stages of John, remain debated. These are approximate composition dates, not dates printed on autographs. Nor are they the dates of the oldest surviving manuscript copies. The introductions to Matthew, Luke and John explain this conventional framework; Dale Martin's discussion of Mark illustrates disagreement over its precise relation to the war and the destruction of the Temple. Markan priority is the widely accepted judgment that Matthew and Luke used Mark, not a claim that Mark is the earliest Christian document or that every tradition it contains originated with its author. Arguments concern patterns of wording, sequence, omissions and editorial changes. The relationship between Matthew and Luke remains disputed: the Two-Source hypothesis uses Mark and a reconstructed sayings source, Q; the Farrer hypothesis has Luke use Matthew as well as Mark. Accepting Markan priority does not require accepting Q. Mark Goodacre on Markan priority; Stephen C. Carlson's survey of the Synoptic Problem. This chronology supports comparing earlier and later presentations. It does not establish that nobody described a bodily resurrection for fifty years, that all possible witnesses were dead when Matthew was written, or that Mark simply turned Paul's letters into a biography. Those are additional claims requiring additional evidence.

title: Early resurrection accounts and source criticism
heading: What Paul actually supplies
text: In 1 Corinthians 15:3–8, Paul passes on a sequence: Christ died, was buried, was raised and appeared to named individuals and groups, ending with Paul himself. He presents material he had received, so the letter's date is later than at least some of its tradition. Scholars debate the precise boundaries, provenance and age of that inherited material. The passage does not identify the occasion on which Paul received every element. 1 Corinthians 15:3–11 and its textual notes. Paul does not supply the Gospel scene of women finding Joseph of Arimathea's tomb empty. He does not describe wounds being inspected, a meal with the risen Jesus, or the sensory details of the appearances in his list. The five hundred are reported by Paul; we do not possess five hundred independent accounts. An early report and independently corroborated testimony are different kinds of evidence. Yet Paul gives resurrection more than the meaning that a teacher remains influential. His argument is that if Christ has not been raised, his proclamation fails and the dead are lost. Christ's resurrection begins the future defeat of death. The second half of the chapter asks what kind of body the dead will have, contrasting perishability with imperishability and ordinary life with spiritual life. The seed analogy gives interpreters material for both continuity and radical difference. 1 Corinthians 15. Paul calls his gospel a revelation in Galatians 1 and asks whether he has seen Jesus in 1 Corinthians 9:1. These are his own statements, distinct from the later narratives of his encounter in Acts. “Visionary” can describe a revelatory experience, but should not quietly become either a medical diagnosis or a complete explanation of what every earlier disciple experienced. Putting the appearances in one list does not establish identical circumstances. Galatians 1; 1 Corinthians 9.

title: Early resurrection accounts and source criticism
heading: A spiritual body is a disputed concept, not a shortcut
text: The central expression is sōma pneumatikon, conventionally “spiritual body,” contrasted with sōma psychikon, often translated “natural body.” The difficulty is not solved by importing the modern opposition between solid matter and an invisible, immaterial mind. The question is what Paul meant by these descriptions in his own intellectual and religious setting. Tabor: radical difference from ordinary flesh James Tabor emphasizes that resurrection need not mean the revival of a corpse into its previous condition. His discussion challenges the assumption that the later Gospel scenes of wounds and touch define every early Jewish or Christian use of resurrection language. He reads Paul's future body as a different, heavenly mode of existence. Crucially, he explicitly rejects the inference that this means a disembodied surviving soul. Tabor, “Resurrection of the Dead: Old Body or New Body?”. Tabor therefore supports taking the contrast between earthly and heavenly embodiment seriously. Citing him as though he simply says “Paul believed in a ghost” would misrepresent his argument. His broader judgments about how dominant particular resurrection models were remain scholarly interpretations, not conclusions established merely by the English adjective “spiritual.” Ehrman: the same body transformed Bart Ehrman makes a different emphasis explicit. In the publicly accessible opening of “A Gnostic View of Jesus' Resurrection,” he reads Paul as believing that Jesus' corpse itself was transformed into an immortal spiritual body. He distinguishes this from later views in which the body remains dead while the spirit survives. In a follow-up comment, he clarifies that his interpretation of Paul does not imply that Paul knew the Gospel story about women discovering a particular tomb. Ehrman's post and clarification. That is an interpretation of Paul's belief, not Ehrman's affirmation that the miracle occurred. It is also evidence that a skeptical modern historian need not read Paul's “spiritual body” as the abandonment of bodily resurrection. The two debates cannot be mapped onto a simple division between believing and unbelieving scholars. Martin and Wright: a real disagreement about the language Dale Martin places Paul's language against ancient ideas in which pneuma could be a kind of substance. In his Yale lecture, the resurrection body is radically different from ordinary flesh and blood, but still substantial. This challenges the assumption that ancient spiritual existence must mean modern immateriality. Martin, “Paul as Pastor”. N. T. Wright instead emphasizes what animates the body: psychikon and pneumatikon distinguish ordinary mortal life from life empowered by God's Spirit. He resists translating the contrast as physical versus nonphysical. His argument also draws on Romans 8:11, where divine Spirit gives life to mortal bodies. Wright, “Mind, Spirit, Soul and Body”; Romans 8. These readings should not be collapsed into one consensus about the mechanics of transformation. What they jointly expose is the inadequacy of a two-box choice between an unchanged human corpse walking again and an entirely disembodied mind. My original distinction remains worth investigating, but the alternatives must be described more carefully than “spiritual versus literal.” A writer can believe literally in a transformed spiritual body. The contrast between “Greek Paul” and “Hebrew bodily resurrection” is also too sharp. Daniel 12 combines awakening from the dust with radiance like the stars. Jewish resurrection imagery already allowed transformation; Greek vocabulary did not make Paul cease to be a Jewish interpreter of scripture. A genealogy of ideas needs specific texts rather than two uniform civilizations. Daniel 12:1–3.

title: Early resurrection accounts and source criticism
heading: Paul's conflicts do not establish total rejection
text: The archived proposal also connects Paul's revelation with rejection by the Jerusalem apostles. Galatians gives a more complicated picture. Paul claims independence, describes visiting Cephas and James, reports recognition of his mission by James, Cephas and John, and recounts a confrontation with Cephas over table fellowship. His account is interested and argumentative, but it is evidence for both cooperation and conflict. Galatians 1–2. The claim that these apostles nicknamed Paul “Simon Magus” is not supplied by these letters. Identifying Paul behind a later literary opponent requires its own argument from the dates, sources and aims of those texts. It cannot be inserted into Paul's biography as an established event. Likewise, an exact interval of seven years between Jesus' death and Paul's revelation is not established by the passages discussed here.

title: Early resurrection accounts and source criticism
heading: Mark's endings: three questions that must stay separate
text: What does Mark 16:1–8 say? The women visit the tomb, encounter a young man, hear that Jesus has been raised and are directed toward a future meeting in Galilee. They flee in fear. Jesus does not appear as a character in this surviving scene, but resurrection is explicitly announced. “Mark contains no resurrection” is therefore inaccurate. “The earliest recoverable ending contains no narrated appearance of the risen Jesus” identifies the actual difference. Mark 16:1–8. What was added during transmission? The fourth-century Greek codices Vaticanus and Sinaiticus end at 16:8. Other witnesses transmit further material. The familiar Longer Ending is 16:9–20. The technical term “Shorter Ending” usually names a separate brief addition after 16:8, not merely the Gospel ending at verse 8. There is also an expansion within the Longer Ending known as the Freer Logion. The USCCB text and notes display the different endings. H. A. G. Houghton's recent study describes the editorial consensus that the earliest attainable text ends at 16:8. It reassesses two medieval catena manuscripts, GA 304, often cited in earlier discussions, and GA 239, not previously prominent in them. Neither should count as evidence for the ending represented by Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Their physical and commentary histories matter, not just where the surviving text stops. This is a useful example of criticism revising its own evidence rather than merely counting manuscripts. Houghton, “Unfinished Business,” New Testament Studies 69 (2023), 35–42; accessible article PDF. The Longer Ending is nevertheless ancient. Irenaeus cites its ascension statement as Mark's conclusion around the late second century. Its presence in most later Greek copies is real evidence of reception, though numerical predominance among surviving copies does not by itself determine the earliest wording. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.10.5; James Kelhoffer's study of the early evidence. Did the author intend the abrupt ending? Recovering an early text and recovering an author's intention are different tasks. Some interpreters see 16:8 as a deliberate literary ending that confronts the reader with fear, failed response and an unfulfilled promise. Others propose that an original conclusion was lost. A lost ending remains a hypothesis; we do not possess it. Establishing that 16:9–20 is secondary does not automatically decide between those possibilities. Martin's discussion of Mark's ending. Canonical authority is another question. A church may receive the Longer Ending as scripture while acknowledging its distinct composition history. The Catholic notes linked above do exactly that. Historical authorship, earliest recoverable wording and a community's judgment about its canon should not be treated as interchangeable verdicts.

title: Early resurrection accounts and source criticism
heading: What becomes more tangible in the later Gospels?
text: The differences are visible without constructing a single harmonized account. In Matthew 28, women grasp Jesus' feet, and the disciples encounter him in Galilee. Matthew also includes a dispute about the removal of the body. These details are absent from Paul's appearance list and Mark 16:1–8. Matthew 28. Luke 24 gives the contrast unusual force: the disciples fear that they see a spirit; Jesus points to his flesh and bones, invites touch and eats fish. Yet the same chapter has him vanish after recognition at Emmaus. Luke's story combines bodily continuity with extraordinary capacities. Calling it an ordinary resuscitation would overlook part of what the text narrates. Luke 24:13–43. Paul's “flesh and blood can't inherit God's Kingdom” in 1 Corinthians 15:50 and Luke's “flesh and bones” in 24:39 deserve direct comparison. Paul is discussing the transition from perishable existence to imperishable resurrection life. Luke is narrating Jesus' response to disciples who mistake him for a spirit: the bodily language establishes his tangible identity. A continuity reading interprets Paul's phrase as mortal humanity in its present condition and Luke's as embodied identity after transformation. A development reading emphasizes how much more explicitly Luke insists on palpable flesh. The different contexts help explain the language, but they do not make the difference disappear or establish that the writers imagined precisely the same thing. Nor does the change from “blood” to “bones” supply an anatomical account of the risen body. 1 Corinthians 15:35–54; Luke 24:36–43. John 20 likewise identifies the risen Jesus through wounds while describing his presence among disciples behind locked doors. Thomas is invited to examine the wounds; the narrative does not explicitly say that he actually touches them. The episode culminates in belief, including the position of later readers who have not seen. John 20. The doubt and failures of recognition are themselves part of the question. Matthew 28:17 places worship beside doubt. Luke 24:16 says the travelers' eyes are kept from recognizing Jesus, while 24:37–43 moves from fear of a spirit through bodily demonstration to astonished disbelief. John 20:14–16 has Mary mistake Jesus for the gardener until he addresses her by name; 20:24–29 gives Thomas an explicit demand for evidence. These are distinct literary depictions of recognition, uncertainty and persuasion, not a uniform report of effortless identification. They may invite historical questions about the experiences behind the stories, but they do not independently establish those experiences' causes. Doubt is neither automatic proof that the encounters were invented nor automatic proof that they happened because an author included an awkward detail. Matthew 28; Luke 24; John 20. These scenes support the observation that later surviving narratives make tangible identity much more explicit. It is reasonable to investigate apologetic purposes, remembered traditions and literary development. It is a further inference to say that their authors invented all such material specifically to overturn Paul's doctrine. The texts do not announce that project. Luke's opposition to mistaking Jesus for a spirit is direct evidence; an exact reconstruction of the opponents or sources behind it is less secure. Nor does the date of a Gospel settle the age of each tradition within it. A later author can preserve older material, elaborate it, combine it with scripture, or introduce new scenes. Source criticism must make the case passage by passage. “Later” is an important observation, but it cannot do all that explanatory work alone.

title: Early resurrection accounts and source criticism
heading: The virgin birth: a parallel question, with different evidence
text: Matthew 1 and Luke 1 explicitly attribute Jesus' conception to divine action without sexual relations. Their infancy narratives differ in presentation: Matthew's announcement is to Joseph in a dream, while Luke's is to Mary through Gabriel. The shared claim deserves attention, but the two narratives should first be read separately rather than combined into a familiar Christmas sequence. Matthew 1:18–25; Luke 1:26–38. Paul does not explicitly teach a virginal conception. Galatians 4:4 says that God's Son was born of a woman and under the law. That wording supplies neither a virgin-birth story nor an explicit rejection of one. Mark begins with Jesus' adult ministry; John's prologue speaks of preexistence and incarnation rather than narrating Mary's conception. Absence from these different kinds of text cannot be converted into a precise date when the belief was invented. Galatians 4; Mark's structure; John's prologue and composition. Matthew's use of Isaiah 7:14 is especially important. In its earlier setting the oracle addresses Ahaz and a contemporary political crisis. Hebrew ‘almah denotes a young woman without itself specifying virginity; the Greek rendering with parthenos provides the wording Matthew applies to Jesus. Distinguishing the earlier context from Matthew's reading makes the interpretive development visible. It does not, by itself, establish whether scripture generated the conception story, was used to interpret an existing tradition, or participated in a more complicated process. Isaiah 7 and the notes on 7:14. The strongest defensible comparison is therefore between different levels of attestation and different literary aims. Matthew and Luke give explicit conception accounts where the earlier surviving sources do not. The further claim that the accounts were consciously fabricated requires an argument beyond their lateness. Equally, their presence in scripture is not independent historical verification of the event they affirm.

title: Early resurrection accounts and source criticism
heading: People noticed problems before modern criticism
text: The manuscript problem at Mark's ending was not discovered only after the Enlightenment. The ad Marinum, transmitted under Eusebius' name, considers both setting aside the disputed ending and harmonizing the apparent difference with Matthew. Kelhoffer stresses its apologetic purpose and the complexity of its testimony. It demonstrates ancient awareness of variants and discrepancies; it should not be turned into a modern census of every manuscript then in existence. Kelhoffer, “The Witness of Eusebius' ad Marinum,” ZNW 92 (2001), 78–112. Modern historical criticism expanded the inquiry into language, authorship, sources and social setting. Spinoza's Theological-Political Treatise (1670) argued for interpreting scripture through its language and historical circumstances rather than treating later doctrinal assumptions as the key to every passage. He was part of a longer interpretive history, not the first human being to notice textual difficulty. Steven Nadler's account of Spinoza and scripture. Reimarus's posthumously published arguments in the eighteenth century distinguished Jesus' aims from those attributed to his followers. Strauss's Life of Jesus (1835–36) made mythical formation central to Gospel interpretation. In this usage, myth did not have to mean a deliberate lie: a community could express religious conviction through stories shaped by inherited scripture. Their particular reconstructions are not binding results of using critical methods. Fernando Bermejo-Rubio's historical survey. This history matters because “critical” is often mistaken for a predetermined rejection of religion, just as “believing” is mistaken for an inability to recognize variation. The actual arguments require examination. An interpreter's religious position does not replace evidence for a reading.

title: Early resurrection accounts and source criticism
heading: A method that does not assume its conclusion
text: For this inquiry, the tasks can be kept distinct: - Textual criticism: What wording is best supported by manuscripts, translations and early quotations? Mark 16 is the clearest example here. - Source criticism: What earlier written or oral material did an author use? Matthew's use of Mark is a different question from Paul's understanding of resurrection. - Form and tradition criticism: How might individual sayings and stories have circulated before their surviving written settings? Reconstructing an earlier stage requires an argument; it does not recover a missing document by assertion. - Redaction criticism: How does an author select, arrange and change material? Added emphasis can be identified more confidently than every motive behind it. - Historical reconstruction: What probably happened, given the nature, date, dependence and limitations of the evidence? - Reception history and theology: How did communities read these texts, and what authority or meaning do they assign to them now? Multiple documents do not automatically equal multiple independent witnesses. A theological purpose does not automatically make every detail false. An earlier source is not automatically exhaustive. Silence matters most when there is good reason to expect the author to mention the missing information. A reconstruction should also identify what evidence would count against it, rather than explaining every possible result as confirmation. Historical investigation can establish that resurrection was proclaimed early and can compare what its advocates meant. Whether a supernatural act is the best explanation requires further judgments about historical inference and the possibility of miracles. Simply recovering an early creed does not settle that issue. Conversely, showing literary development does not amount to a demonstration that no extraordinary event occurred. The same discipline can open a wider comparison involving the Dead Sea Scrolls, Nag Hammadi writings, Sumerian texts, Judaism and Kabbalah. Each comparison still needs its own dates, contexts and evidence of transmission; a resemblance alone does not establish shared origins. A contemporary cross-tradition synthesis can be explored as a constructive project without presenting it as a recovered ancient consensus. The companion chapter takes up that broader possibility.

title: Early resurrection accounts and source criticism
heading: What remains of the original proposal?
text: The evidence preserves the question's force while limiting its strongest formulation. 1. Early resurrection proclamation is securely attested in Paul. Its wording cannot be reduced to a later Gospel scene, but neither does it merely say that Jesus' teachings survived. 2. Paul's resurrection body differs radically from ordinary mortal existence. The precise relation between old and new embodiment remains debated. “Spiritual” alone does not establish disembodiment. 3. Mark's earliest recoverable ending announces resurrection without narrating an appearance. Its textual history is real, ancient and independently worth studying. 4. Later Gospel accounts elaborate tangible encounters. The development of literary presentation is observable; a single proven transition from universally nonbodily belief to invented bodily belief is not. 5. The virgin-conception narratives have a different pattern of attestation. Their absence from earlier surviving texts is relevant, but does not locate their origin with certainty. The resulting inquiry is still substantial: how did communities transmit, interpret and give narrative form to claims about Jesus after his death? Keeping that question open is more productive than requiring every text to mean the same thing, or requiring every difference to prove the whole reconstruction in advance.
